[All benchmarks](../benchmarks.qmd)

A nightly account review must finish before investigators start work. This
benchmark asks how batch size would affect job throughput and batch latency
when the model, transaction histories, and machine stay fixed.

::: {.callout-note title="Fictional benchmark"}
All data, hardware specifications, schemas, and results on this page are
fictional placeholders. No benchmark has been run.
:::

## Example

One Parquet row is an account at a common review cutoff. This fictional
eight-transaction observation belongs to the short-history part of the
proposed workload. Records are oldest to newest and all are known by the
May 28, 2026 at 14:30 cutoff.

```yaml
account_id: account-42
trxns:
  - booked_at: "2026-05-19T08:00:00"
    amount: 4.50
    merchant: Station Cafe
  - booked_at: "2026-05-20T17:30:00"
    amount: 28.10
    merchant: North Market
  - booked_at: "2026-05-21T10:00:00"
    amount: 32.00
    merchant: Station Cafe
  - booked_at: "2026-05-22T12:15:00"
    amount: 12.40
    merchant: River Deli
  - booked_at: "2026-05-24T09:00:00"
    amount: 24.00
    merchant: Harbor Internet
  - booked_at: "2026-05-25T18:45:00"
    amount: 19.80
    merchant: River Deli
  - booked_at: "2026-05-27T18:15:00"
    amount: 56.20
    merchant: North Market
  - booked_at: "2026-05-28T14:30:00"
    amount: 84.50
    merchant: North Market
```

Scoring inputs omit `disputed`. The checkpoint's target predicts whether each
retained transaction receives a new dispute during the 30 days after the
common cutoff. `account_id` remains an application identifier outside the
model schema.

## Schema

The job uses the same small model for every batch-size setting. One account
observation contains one `trxns` list and produces a dispute result for every
retained transaction.

```{typst}
//| label: fig-benchmark-batch-scoring
//| fig-cap: "Fictional scoring schema: each account row contains a transaction history with one dispute target per transaction."
//| fig-alt: "An account root contains the repeated branch trxns. Each transaction contains booked_at DateParts, amount Number, merchant Category, and disputed Boolean. The disputed target is always hidden from input and omitted from the scoring request."
#tree(node("account", kind: "root", children: (
  node("trxns", kind: "branch", repeated: true, children: (
    node("booked_at", type: "DateParts"),
    node("amount", type: "Number"),
    node("merchant", type: "Category"),
    node("disputed", kind: "target", type: "Boolean", body: [Always hidden.]),
  )),
)))
```

<details>
<summary>Complete model schema</summary>

```python
import relflow as rf

model = rf.Model.xs(
    trxns=rf.Branch(
        length=128,
        overflow="tail",
        booked_at=rf.DateParts(
            dateparts=["day_of_month", "day_of_week", "hour_of_day"],
        ),
        amount=rf.Number,
        merchant=rf.Category,
        disputed=rf.Boolean(mask=True),
    ),
)
```

The cap retains at most the last 128 supplied transactions. It is an input
capacity, not a promise of 128 output records per account. Repeated prediction
records use variable Arrow lists containing the retained positions.
`DateParts` provide calendar features rather than elapsed-time gaps.

</details>

## Comparison

Score the same ordered file with batch sizes of 64, 128, and 256 **account
observations**. Keep the checkpoint, precision, hardware, output selection, and
history lengths fixed. Report throughput in account observations per second;
a transaction prediction is a different counting unit.

The proposed timing boundary begins when a warmed scoring loop requests its
next file batch and ends when the corresponding Arrow predictions are ready
in host memory. It includes source reads, preparation, transfers, model work,
and output conversion. It excludes checkpoint loading, warm-up, and writing
the final output file. These are proposed end-to-end batch timings, not isolated
model-kernel timings or online request latency.

## Result

| Batch size, accounts | Mean batch cycle, ms ↓ | Account observations / second ↑ | Timed workload, seconds ↓ |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 64 | 32 | 2,000.0 | 8.192 |
| 128 | 48 | 2,666.7 | 6.144 |
| 256 | 80 | 3,200.0 | 5.120 |

: Fictional placeholder timings for 16,384 account observations. All values are invented; throughput is calculated from the displayed batch cycle. {#tbl-benchmark-batch-scoring-results}

The example trades a longer batch cycle for a shorter scoring job. A measured
comparison would also report peak memory and variation across repeated passes.

<details>
<summary>Proposed workload and timing protocol</summary>

**Fictional source.** The application would supply
`benchmarks/batch-scoring/accounts.parquet`, with 16,384 account observations
and no dispute labels. Define the retained history distribution exactly:

| Account observations | Share | Transactions per account |
| ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 4,096 | 25% | 8 |
| 8,192 | 50% | 32 |
| 4,096 | 25% | 56 |

That is 524,288 retained transactions, averaging 32 per account. The longest
history is 56; the schema's cap of 128 leaves headroom without changing this
workload. Use the same deterministic row order for all batch sizes, including
the same placement of long and short histories. Record that order and the
resulting batch widths: internal padding still costs memory and computation.

**Fictional machine and model.** Reserve one illustrative accelerator with
16 GiB of device memory, eight host CPU cores, 32 GiB of host memory, and local
solid-state storage. Use one process and one device, BF16 model computation,
and the same warmed `xs` checkpoint and fitted preparation state for every
setting.

**Application interface.** Supply the fictional path through the prediction
split of `rf.ArrowDataModule`; set batch size on the prediction loop. The schema
above describes the checkpoint, rather than an untrained model to time:

```python
# model is the application-loaded checkpoint with the schema above.
data = rf.ArrowDataModule(
    model=model,
    predict="benchmarks/batch-scoring/accounts.parquet",
)
predictions = model.predict(datamodule=data, batch_size=128, devices=1)
```

**Timing plan.** Warm the model and source cache before measurement, then run
five complete passes per batch size in a rotated order. Synchronize device
work at the timing boundaries and include batch preparation and Arrow output
conversion. Retain the same default prediction output selection for every
pass. Report run-to-run spread, peak device memory, and full-job elapsed time
alongside throughput when actual runs exist. Cold-start and persisted-output
timings would require separate measurements.

**Arithmetic.** The fictional table uses 256, 128, and 64 batches respectively.
With no partial final batch, total time is batch count times mean batch cycle;
throughput is 16,384 account observations divided by that time. Multiply by
the workload's mean of 32 only when explicitly reporting transaction
predictions per second.

</details>
